english: The palace and the government offices are one and the same body;

in promotions and punishments, in praise and blame, there should be no difference. If any commit crimes and break the law, or prove loyal and good, let them be handed to the proper officials to judge their reward or penalty, so as to show Your Majesty's just and enlightened governance;
there should be no partiality, making the laws different inside and outside the palace.
To be close to worthy ministers and keep petty men at a distance—this is why the Earlier Han flourished;
to be close to petty men and keep worthy ministers at a distance—this is why the Later Han collapsed.
I was originally a commoner, tilling my own fields at Nanyang, seeking only to preserve my life in troubled times, not striving to be known among the feudal lords.
I beg Your Majesty to entrust me with the task of defeating the traitors and restoring the Han; if I fail, then punish my crime, and report it to the spirit of the late Emperor.
If no words come for the advancement of virtue, then blame the negligence of You, Zhi, Yun and the others, to make their fault plain;
Your Majesty too should plan for yourself, seek out good counsel, examine and accept worthy advice, and deeply honour the late Emperor's testamentary edict.
I am overwhelmed with gratitude for the grace I have received.
Now that I am about to depart afar, facing this memorial my tears fall—I know not what I say.
He rowed upstream along the stream, forgetting how far he had gone.
Suddenly he came upon a peach grove flanking the banks for several hundred paces, with no other trees among it; the fragrant grass was fresh and lovely, and fallen petals drifted in profusion.
The fisherman was greatly amazed.
He went further on, wishing to reach the end of the grove.
Where the grove ended at the stream's source he found a mountain, with a small opening that seemed to let in light.
So he left his boat and entered through the opening.
After a few dozen more steps, it suddenly opened out into brightness.
The land was level and broad, the houses neat and orderly, with fertile fields, fine ponds, mulberries, bamboos and the like.
Paths criss-crossed the fields, and the sounds of cocks and dogs could be heard between neighbours.
There people tilled and went about their work; men and women were dressed like people outside.
White-haired elders and children with hanging hair all lived in happy contentment.
Seeing the fisherman, they were greatly astonished and asked where he came from.
Then they invited him home, set out wine, killed a chicken and prepared food.
When the village heard of this man, they all came to question him.

They told him their ancestors had fled the disorders of the Qin era, bringing wives, children and fellow villagers to this isolated place, never leaving it again, and so had become cut off from the outside world.
This man told them all he had heard, item by item, and they all sighed with regret.
The people of this place said: "It is not worth telling outsiders about."
Once out, he found his boat and followed the old route back, marking the way everywhere.
At the prefecture seat he called on the governor and told him all this.
The governor at once sent men to follow him; they sought the marks he had made, lost their way, and could never find the road again.
Liu Ziji of Nanyang, a gentleman of lofty character, hearing of it, cheerfully planned to go; he died of illness before succeeding.
Afterwards no one asked the way there anymore.
Westward from the hillock I walked a hundred and twenty paces; screened by a grove of bamboo, I heard the sound of water like the tinkling of jade pendants, and my heart delighted in it.
Cutting bamboo to make a path, I looked down and saw a small pool, its water exceptionally clear and cold.
The whole pool is floored by one stone; near the shore the curved stone bottom curls up, forming islets, islelets, crags and rocks of various shapes.
Green trees and kingfisher vines intertwine, droop and sway, unevenly fluttering.
There may be about a hundred fish in the pool, all seeming to swim in empty air with nothing to rest on; the sunlight pierces straight to the bottom, and their shadows spread on the stones.
They stand still as if transfixed, then dart suddenly far away, coming and going swift and light.
As if sharing the joy of the visitors.
Looking southwest from the pool, the stream twists like the Big Dipper and winds like a snake, now visible, now hidden.
Its banks interlock like dogs' teeth, and one cannot know its source.
Sitting above the pool, with bamboo and trees enclosing it on all sides, solitary and empty of people, it chills the spirit and freezes the bone, mournful, still and profound.
Because the place was too bleak, I could not stay long, so I recorded it and left.
Those who travelled with me: Wu Wuling, Gong Gu, and my younger brother Zongxuan.
The attendants who followed were two young men of the Cui family, called Shuji and Fengyi.
